title: On-call and Incident Response Playbook
author: Avery Chen
body:
Overview

This playbook documents Redwood Inference's on-call and incident response practices. It is intended to be the single canonical reference for: incident severity definitions and routing, on-call rotations, operational runbooks, postmortem process, game day planning, and customer communications / status-page templates. Owners are expected to keep runbooks for their services up-to-date and link them from the Runbooks index.

Purpose and scope
- Provide a clearly documented, repeatable incident response process for all production services (hosted API, dedicated pools, private deployments).
- Reduce time-to-detection and time-to-resolution while minimizing customer impact and post-incident toil.
- Define roles, responsibilities, and escalation paths.

Quick links
- Runbook index: confluence/eng-sre/runbook-index
- PagerDuty schedules: https://pagerduty.company/redwood
- Status page: https://status.redwood.ai

1) Incident lifecycle and severity definitions

Severity levels
1. Sev0 (SEV0) - Major outage: entire platform or large customer-facing outage (e.g., hosted API 5xx > 50% traffic). Immediate page and full incident response.
2. Sev1 (SEV1) - Service degradation: significant performance degradation/loss of capacity for one or more critical services (e.g., sustained latency > 2x SLO for > 10 minutes). Full incident response.
3. Sev2 (SEV2) - Partial impairment: localized errors, reduced throughput, or feature-level regressions that affect a small subset of customers. Triage during business hours; escalate if impact grows.
4. Sev3 (SEV3) - Informational/Minor: non-customer-facing errors, internal telemetry anomalies, or scheduled maintenance. Document and resolve in normal workflow.

Detection and initial triage (0-15 minutes)
1. PagerDuty/alert triggers: on-call engineer receives alert.
2. Acknowledge in PagerDuty within 5 minutes.
3. Run initial triage checklist (below). If severity appears Sev1/Sev0, page the wider incident channel and incident commander.

Initial triage checklist (first responder)
- Identify affected service(s) and regions.
- Check SLO dashboards and traffic graphs.
- Gather key identifiers: incident id (create one if none), affected endpoints, error rates, recent deploys.
- Determine initial severity (Sev0/1/2/3).
- Note temporary mitigation if available (restart, scale, failover).
- If Sev1/0, appoint Incident Commander (IC) and open an incident bridge (Zoom/Meet) and an incident Slack channel.

2) Roles and responsibilities

- PagerDuty responder / First responder: acknowledges alert, completes triage checklist, assigns severity.
- Incident Commander (IC): overall coordination, stakeholder communication, and decisions about customer communications and escalations.
- Triage Lead / Engineering Lead: organizes technical responders, assigns investigation tasks.
- SRE Runbook Owner: executes runbook steps; provides mitigation (scaling, restarts, rollbacks).
- Customer Success / Support Lead: prepares and approves customer-facing messages.
- Security Lead (if applicable): engaged immediately for incidents involving data exposure.

Escalation matrix
- If the first responder cannot contain/mitigate within 15 minutes for Sev1/Sev0, escalate to the on-call SRE and then IC.
- For Sev0, notify CTO and on-call product/security leads within 10 minutes.

3) Runbooks and playbooks (template and example)

Runbook template (fields each service runbook must include)
- Service name
- Owner and secondary owner (team and email/PagerDuty role)
- SLOs / metrics to watch (latency p95, error rate, throughput)
- PagerDuty trigger thresholds
- Quick mitigation steps (order matters):
  1. Identify & tag impacted components
  2. Apply temporary mitigation (scale/restart/traffic-shift)
  3. Apply permanent fix or rollback plan
- Common failure modes and diagnostic commands
- CLI commands / k8s manifests to inspect and remediate
- Rollback steps with RBAC/approval notes
- Postmortem checklist and template link

Example runbook: model-serving-degradation
- Owners: Model Serving Team (oncall: model-serving@schedule)
- SLOs: API latency p95 < 250ms, 5xx rate < 0.5%
- PagerDuty triggers: p95 > 400ms for 10m, 5xx > 2% for 5m

Step 0 - Triage
- Check dashboards: grafana/dashboards/model-serving-overview
- Confirm scope: specific model(s), region, or global.
- Check recent deploys: git commit and CI pipeline.
- Check autoscaling: k8s HPA status, GPU pool utilization.

Step 1 - Quick mitigations (ordered)
1. If CPU/GPU saturation: increase pool temporarily (ci/cd scale-gpu-pool --size +2) or shift traffic to dedicated pools.
2. If KV cache miss storms: enable cache-warmup script (scripts/cache_warmup.sh --models x).
3. If model regression suspected: revert last deployment to previous stable revision (kubectl rollout undo deployment/model-serving).
4. If region-specific: failover traffic to another region (runbook: traffic-shift).

Diagnostics (commands)
- kubectl get pods -n model-serving -o wide
- k9s for quick pod diagnostics
- rg "ERROR" /var/log/model-serving/*.log | tail -n 200
- redis-cli -h cache-cluster info

Rollback checklist
- Confirm suspect deploy and commit id.
- Notify IC and Customer Success before rollback if visible to customers.
- Execute: kubectl rollout undo deployment/model-serving --to-revision=<n>
- Monitor error rate and latency for 15 minutes after rollback.

Runbook maintenance
- Owners must review runbook quarterly and after each Sev1/Sev0 incident.

4) Post-incident process and postmortem template

When to write a postmortem
- All Sev1 and Sev0 incidents require a written postmortem within 7 business days.
- Sev2 incidents are reviewed at the discretion of the IC or SRE lead.

Postmortem template (to be published under confluence/incidents)
- Title: Postmortem: <short-desc> - INCIDENT_ID - YYYY-MM-DD
- Summary: one-paragraph customer-facing summary
- Impact: affected services, customers, duration, SLI impact (numbers)
- Timeline: ordered bullets with timestamps (UTC) and actor
- Root cause: short and technical
- Detection: how it was detected (alert, customer report, telemetry)
- Contributing factors: systemic issues and latent conditions
- Mitigations applied: immediate and follow-up actions
- Long-term fixes (owner + ETA)
- Action items (owner, due date, verification criteria)
- Follow-ups: link to runbook updates and test plans
- Severity: final severity level and rationale

Postmortem expectations and review
- Postmortem author is typically the IC or the SRE oncall with domain expertise.
- The postmortem is reviewed by the service owner, SRE manager, and product manager.
- Action items should be tracked in JIRA and linked in the postmortem.

5) On-call rotations and schedules

Structure
- Primary on-call: handles PagerDuty alerts and initial triage (team-level rotation).
- Secondary/backup on-call: receives escalations and provides additional capacity.
- SRE on-call: escalates for platform-level issues and cross-service incidents.

Rotation cadence and expectations
- Typical rotation: 1-week shifts for engineering teams; 2-week shifts for SREs (example, configurable by team).
- Handoff notes: outgoing on-call must publish a Handoff note at start/end of shift with outstanding issues and maintenance windows.
- On-call compensation and time-off: see company handbook; escalate conflicts to manager.

On-call runbook upkeep
- Every team must maintain a README: oncall/README.md with escalation steps and known flaky alerts.
- Quarterly audits: SRE rotation lead verifies schedules and on-call ownership.

6) Game days and runbook drills

Purpose
- Validate runbooks, surface gaps, and train responders without customer impact.

Game day cadence and structure
- Frequency: quarterly for major services, bi-annually for lower-traffic services.
- Participants: service owners, SRE, support, product, security (as needed).
- Scenario design: simulate Sev1/Sev0 and follow through detection, mitigation, and postmortem.
- Success criteria: <30m to detect, <60m to apply mitigation, complete post-exercise retro within 5 business days.

Game day checklist
1. Pre-game: schedule, objectives, and safety rules (ensure route for immediate abort).
2. Inject: synthetic traffic or fault (e.g., pod kill, region failover).
3. Observe: measure detection and mitigation times, note manual steps.
4. Retro: document gaps and owners for runbook updates.

7) Status page and customer communications templates

Status page policy
- Sev0/Sev1 incidents affecting customer experience must have an initial status page entry within 30 minutes of incident declaration.
- Update cadence: every 30 minutes while active, then at major milestones (mitigation, resolution, investigation ongoing).

Status page entry template (initial)
- Title: SERVICE_NAME incident: {brief impact}
- Incident ID: INCIDENT_{YYYYMMDD}_{NN}
- Time detected: 2026-03-04T15:12Z (UTC)
- Impact: Short statement of affected customers and functionality
- Current status: Investigating / Identified / Mitigating / Resolved
- Next update: in 30 minutes
- Contact: support@redwood.ai

Customer email template (initial)
Subject: Incident {INCIDENT_ID} - {SERVICE_NAME} degraded\\n

Hello {CustomerName},

We are investigating an incident affecting {SERVICE_NAME}. Some requests may experience increased latency or errors. Our on-call team has been engaged and we are working to identify the root cause. We will send updates via {status page link} and email every 30 minutes while we have new information.

Impact: {short description}
Estimated time to next update: 30 minutes

We apologize for the disruption and will follow up with a full postmortem.

Sincerely,
Redwood Inference Support

Customer email template (post-resolution)
Subject: Incident {INCIDENT_ID} resolved - {SERVICE_NAME}

Hello {CustomerName},

The incident affecting {SERVICE_NAME} (Incident ID: {INCIDENT_ID}) has been resolved as of {resolved_time}. The service is operating normally. We will publish a full postmortem with root cause analysis and corrective actions within 7 business days.

If you are experiencing continued issues, please contact support@redwood.ai.

Thank you for your patience.

8) Communications & stakeholder updates

- IC is responsible for internal stakeholder updates (weekly exec ping for Sev0 incidents until resolved).
- Customer Success coordinates customer outreach and legal/enterprise escalation for enterprise customers.
- Security team must be looped immediately for incidents involving PII/data access.

9) Metrics, SLOs, and tooling

- Key SLOs to monitor in incidents: request latency (p50/p95/p99), 5xx rate, successful tokens per second for streaming endpoints, queue depth and GPU utilization.
- Dashboards: grafana/service-overview, datadog/error-traces, jaeger/service-traces.
- Alerting thresholds and dampening: avoid noisy alerts - require sustained violation windows (e.g., >5m for p95 breach).

10) Templates and checklists (copyable)

Incident channel naming: incident-INCIDENT_{YYYYMMDD}_{NN}
Incident bridge: meet.google.com/incident-{ID} or Zoom
Incident start checklist:
1. Create incident record and ID in confluence/incidents.
2. Assign severity and IC.
3. Open incident channel and bridge.
4. Post initial status page entry (if Sev1/Sev0).
5. Begin timeline logging.

Incident close checklist:
1. Confirm service stability for 60 minutes (or agreed SLO window).
2. Notify stakeholders and customers via status page/email.
3. Draft postmortem and assign action items.
4. Schedule postmortem review meeting and publish findings.
